CurrentLocation: Vorderasiatisches Museum, Berlin, Germany; British Museum, London; Egyptian Museum, Cairo
Description: About 380 clay tablets in Akkadian cuneiform, the diplomatic correspondence between Pharaohs Amenhotep III and Akhenaten and the kings of Babylon, Assyria, and the city-states of Canaan. Canaanite rulers plead for Egyptian troops against rivals and against raiders they call Habiru.
BiblicalSignificance: The letters open a window on Canaan just before or around the time many scholars place Israel's entry into the land, naming Jerusalem, Shechem, Megiddo, Lachish, and Hazor and their kings. Whether the Habiru are the Hebrews is debated, but the letters confirm the Bible's picture of a fragmented Canaan of city-states awaiting a new chapter.
Interpretations: Scholars agree the letters are genuine fourteenth-century diplomatic correspondence; debate centers on the ‘Habiru’ named in them — whether they have any connection to the Hebrews is unproven.
